e: Fat yields about 9 kcal per gram, more than double that of carbohydrate or protein.

e: Both carbohydrate and protein supply about 4 kcal per gram.

e: Proteins are made up of amino acids.

s: Section J - Social Work

q: In Maslow's hierarchy of needs, which need is at the base?
e: Physiological needs (food, water, shelter) form the base of Maslow's hierarchy.
s: Section J - Social Work

q: A 'coping mechanism' refers to:
o: A way of dealing with stress or problems
e: Coping mechanisms are the strategies people use to manage stress and difficulties.
s: Section J - Social Work

q: The first school of social work in India (founded 1936) is today known as:
e: The Sir Dorabji Tata Graduate School of Social Work (1936) is now the Tata Institute of Social Sciences.
s: Section J - Social Work

q: Social policy is mainly concerned with:
o: Government principles and action for social welfare
e: Social policy covers the principles and actions of government aimed at promoting social welfare.
s: Section J - Social Work

q: Which model of social work practice views the person within their environment as a 'system'?
e: The systems approach sees the individual interacting with family, community and society as systems.
s: Section J - Social Work

q: Rehabilitation, correctional services and probation come under the field of:
e: Social defence deals with prevention of crime and the care and rehabilitation of offenders.
s: Section J - Social Work

q: The term 'Sociology' was coined by:
e: Auguste Comte coined the term 'Sociology' and is called the Father of Sociology.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: Auguste Comte is popularly known as the:
e: Comte is regarded as the Father of Sociology.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: Comte's 'Law of Three Stages' holds that human thought passes through the theological, the metaphysical and the:
e: The three stages are theological, metaphysical and positive (scientific).
s: Section K - Sociology

q: 'Positivism', the use of scientific methods to study society, is associated with:
e: Comte advocated positivism, applying scientific observation to social phenomena.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: The 'organic analogy', comparing society to a living organism, was given by:
e: Herbert Spencer compared society to a biological organism in his organic analogy.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: 'Survival of the fittest' applied to social evolution is associated with:
e: Herbert Spencer extended evolutionary ideas to society (Social Darwinism).
s: Section K - Sociology

q: The central idea of Karl Marx's social theory is the:
e: Marx held that the history of society is the history of class struggle.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: Marx's view that economic factors determine the structure of society is called:
e: Economic determinism holds that the economic base shapes the social superstructure.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: According to Marx, capitalist society is mainly divided into the bourgeoisie and the:
e: Marx divided capitalist society into the bourgeoisie (owners) and the proletariat (workers).
s: Section K - Sociology

q: Social stratification refers to:
o: The division of society into a hierarchy of layers or strata
e: Stratification is the arrangement of society into ranked layers or strata.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: The caste system is an example of which type of stratification?
o: Closed system based on ascribed status
e: Caste is a closed system; status is ascribed by birth, with little mobility.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: The class system, unlike caste, is based mainly on:
e: Class position is largely achieved and based on economic and social attainment.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: Which of the following is NOT a primary agent of socialisation?
e: Family, peer group, school and mass media are agents of socialisation; the stock exchange is not.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: The most important primary agent of socialisation in early life is the:
e: The family is the first and most influential agent of socialisation.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: Control exercised through laws, courts and the police is an example of:
e: Formal social control operates through codified laws and official agencies.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: Customs, traditions, folkways and public opinion are forms of:
e: Informal social control works through unwritten norms, customs and public opinion.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: A family consisting only of parents and their unmarried children is called a:
e: A nuclear family comprises a couple and their dependent children.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: A household in which parents, married children and other kin live together is a:
e: A joint or extended family includes several related generations living together.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: Marriage to only one spouse at a time is called:
e: Monogamy is marriage to a single spouse at a time.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: A form of marriage in which one man has more than one wife at the same time is:
e: Polygyny is one man married to several wives; polyandry is one woman with several husbands.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: The Dowry Prohibition Act in India was enacted in:
e: The Dowry Prohibition Act was passed in 1961, making the giving or taking of dowry an offence.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: Kudumbashree, a large women's self-help network in Kerala, mainly aims at:
o: Women's economic empowerment and poverty eradication
e: Kudumbashree empowers women economically and works to eradicate poverty through self-help groups.
s: Section K - Sociology

q: Psychology is best defined as the scientific study of:
e: Modern psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes.
s: Section L - Psychology: Foundations, Biological Basis & Motivation

q: The first psychology laboratory (1879) was established by:
e: Wilhelm Wundt set up the first psychology laboratory at Leipzig in 1879.
s: Section L - Psychology: Foundations, Biological Basis & Motivation

q: The capacity of short-term memory is about:
e: Miller's 'magic number' describes short-term memory capacity as about 7 +/- 2 items.
s: Section L - Psychology: Foundations, Biological Basis & Motivation

q: The memory store that holds sensory information for a very brief instant is:
e: Sensory memory briefly retains raw sensory input before it is processed.
s: Section L - Psychology: Foundations, Biological Basis & Motivation

q: The Intelligence Quotient (IQ) is calculated as:
e: Ratio IQ = (Mental Age / Chronological Age) x 100.
s: Section L - Psychology: Foundations, Biological Basis & Motivation

q: The first practical intelligence test was developed by:
e: Alfred Binet (with Simon) devised the first practical intelligence test in 1905.
s: Section L - Psychology: Foundations, Biological Basis & Motivation

q: The basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system is the:
e: The neuron (nerve cell) is the basic unit of the nervous system.
s: Section L - Psychology: Foundations, Biological Basis & Motivation

q: The junction across which a nerve impulse passes from one neuron to another is the:
e: The synapse is the gap between neurons across which impulses are transmitted.
s: Section L - Psychology: Foundations, Biological Basis & Motivation

q: Chemical substances that carry impulses across the synapse are called:
e: Neurotransmitters are the chemical messengers that cross the synaptic gap.
s: Section L - Psychology: Foundations, Biological Basis & Motivation

q: The part of the brain mainly responsible for balance and coordination of movement is the:
e: The cerebellum controls balance, posture and the coordination of voluntary movement.
s: Section L - Psychology: Foundations, Biological Basis & Motivation

q: The 'master gland' of the endocrine system is the:
e: The pituitary gland is called the master gland because it regulates other endocrine glands.
s: Section L - Psychology: Foundations, Biological Basis & Motivation

q: Hunger, thirst and sleep are examples of:
e: Hunger, thirst and sleep are biological or primary motives rooted in physiological needs.
s: Section L - Psychology: Foundations, Biological Basis & Motivation

q: At the top of Maslow's hierarchy of needs is:
e: Self-actualisation, the realisation of one's potential, is the highest need in Maslow's hierarchy.
s: Section L - Psychology: Foundations, Biological Basis & Motivation

q: The 'fight or flight' response to a threat is controlled mainly by the:
e: The sympathetic nervous system mobilises the body for 'fight or flight' under stress.
s: Section L - Psychology: Foundations, Biological Basis & Motivation

q: The General Adaptation Syndrome, describing the stages of stress (alarm, resistance, exhaustion), was proposed by:
e: Hans Selye described the General Adaptation Syndrome as the body's response to prolonged stress.
s: Section L - Psychology: Foundations, Biological Basis & Motivation

q: Sigmund Freud's theory of development is known as the theory of:
e: Freud proposed stages of psychosexual development driven by libido.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: The first stage in Freud's psychosexual theory is the:
e: The oral stage (birth to about one year) is the first of Freud's psychosexual stages.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: Erik Erikson's theory is known as the theory of:
e: Erikson proposed eight stages of psychosocial development across the lifespan.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: The first psychosocial crisis in Erikson's theory (infancy) is:
e: In infancy the crisis is trust vs. mistrust, resolved through reliable caregiving.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: Jean Piaget is best known for his theory of:
e: Piaget described how children's thinking develops through cognitive stages.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: The first stage of Piaget's cognitive development (birth to about 2 years) is the:
e: In the sensorimotor stage infants learn through senses and motor actions.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: The understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight ('object permanence') develops in the:
e: Object permanence is acquired during the sensorimotor stage.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: Lawrence Kohlberg is known for his theory of:
e: Kohlberg proposed stages of moral reasoning from pre-conventional to post-conventional levels.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: The concept of the 'Zone of Proximal Development' was given by:
e: Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development is the gap between what a child can do alone and with help.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: The theory of attachment between infant and caregiver was developed by:
e: John Bowlby's attachment theory stresses the early emotional bond with the caregiver.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: Classical conditioning, demonstrated with dogs salivating to a bell, is associated with:
e: Ivan Pavlov demonstrated classical conditioning in his experiments with dogs.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: Operant conditioning, based on reinforcement and punishment, is associated with:
e: B.F. Skinner developed operant conditioning, shaping behaviour through consequences.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: Learning by observing and imitating others (social learning theory) is associated with:
e: Albert Bandura's social learning theory emphasises observational learning, shown in the Bobo doll study.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: ADHD, a common childhood disorder, stands for:
e: ADHD is Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, marked by inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: Repeated involuntary urination (bed-wetting) beyond the expected age is clinically called:
e: Enuresis is repeated involuntary urination, often at night, past the age of bladder control.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: Repeated involuntary passing of faeces in inappropriate places by a child is called:
e: Encopresis is the repeated, often involuntary, passing of stool in inappropriate places.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: Autism Spectrum Disorder mainly affects a child's:
e: Autism is a developmental disorder affecting social communication, interaction and behaviour.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: Changing one's behaviour or opinion to match those of a group is called:
e: Conformity is adjusting one's behaviour or attitudes to align with group norms.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: An unjustified, usually negative, attitude held towards the members of a group is called:
e: Prejudice is a preconceived negative attitude; discrimination is the unfair behaviour that may follow it.
s: Section M - Psychology: Development, Social & Abnormal

q: A 4-year-old has severe muscle wasting, very low weight, a wrinkled 'old man' face, but NO swelling. This indicates:
e: Marasmus shows severe wasting of muscle and fat without oedema.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: A child shows pitting oedema of the legs, a puffy 'moon' face and skin changes, with fat fairly preserved. This indicates:
e: Kwashiorkor is protein deficiency marked by oedema (swelling) and skin/hair changes.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: The anterior fontanelle (the 'soft spot' on a baby's head) normally closes by about:
e: The anterior fontanelle usually closes by about 18 months of age.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: A newborn turns its head and opens its mouth when its cheek is gently touched. This reflex is the:
e: The rooting reflex helps the newborn locate the nipple for feeding.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: When support is suddenly removed, a newborn flings out its arms and then draws them in. This is the:
e: The Moro or startle reflex is a normal newborn response to a sudden loss of support.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: Two-word ('telegraphic') speech such as 'mama go' typically appears at about:
e: Telegraphic, two-word speech generally emerges around 18-24 months.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: A 2-year-old insists on feeding herself and frequently says 'no'. In Erikson's theory she is resolving:
e: The toddler stage centres on autonomy vs. shame and doubt.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: A 7-year-old realises that water poured into a taller, thinner glass is still the same amount. He has acquired:
e: Conservation, the understanding that quantity stays the same despite changes in shape, marks the concrete operational stage.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: Low birth weight is defined as a birth weight of less than:
e: A baby weighing under 2,500 g at birth is classified as low birth weight.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: A 9-month-old cries and clings to his mother when a stranger tries to hold him. This is:
e: Stranger anxiety, fear of unfamiliar people, is normal around 8-9 months.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: Complementary (weaning) foods should be introduced alongside breast milk starting at:
e: Complementary feeding should begin at 6 months, when breast milk alone is no longer sufficient.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: 'Exclusive breastfeeding' means giving the infant:
o: Only breast milk and nothing else
e: Exclusive breastfeeding means only breast milk, with no other food or even water.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: Under the immunization schedule, the first dose of measles vaccine is given at about:
e: The first dose of measles-containing vaccine is given at about 9 months.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: Kangaroo Mother Care (skin-to-skin contact) is recommended mainly for:
e: Kangaroo Mother Care helps keep low-birth-weight and preterm babies warm and stable.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: A 3-year-old talks to her doll as if it were alive and feeds it pretend food. Per Piaget this reflects:
e: Symbolic, make-believe play and animism are typical of Piaget's preoperational stage.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: A baby usually begins to crawl at about:
e: Crawling typically begins around 8-10 months.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: Copying a square and hopping on one foot are motor milestones typical of a child aged about:
e: These fine and gross motor skills are usually mastered around 4-5 years.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: A 1-year-old waves 'bye-bye' and claps in imitation of adults. This mainly shows development of:
e: Waving and imitating gestures reflect early social and imitative development.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: Human development generally proceeds in a manner that is:
o: Orderly and follows a predictable sequence
Identical in timing for all children
e: Development follows an orderly, predictable sequence, though the pace varies between children.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: A child who can walk upstairs one step at a time at around two years is showing a:
e: Walking upstairs uses large muscles and is a gross motor milestone.
s: Section N - Child Development: Applied & Extended

q: Deficiency of Vitamin B12 chiefly causes:
e: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: Vitamin K is essential mainly for:
e: Vitamin K is required for normal blood clotting.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: Deficiency of riboflavin (Vitamin B2) commonly causes:
e: Riboflavin deficiency causes cracks at the corners of the mouth (angular stomatitis) and cheilosis.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: Pellagra, with dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia, is caused by deficiency of:
e: Niacin (B3) deficiency causes pellagra, classically the 'three Ds'.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: Which is a rich natural source of Vitamin C?
e: Amla, guava and citrus fruits are rich in Vitamin C.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: A pregnant woman is prescribed 'IFA' tablets at the Anganwadi. IFA stands for:
e: IFA (Iron and Folic Acid) tablets prevent anaemia in pregnancy.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: Excess fluoride in drinking water causes:
e: Long-term excess fluoride causes dental and skeletal fluorosis.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: Many children in a low-sunlight locality show bow legs and delayed walking. The likely deficiency is:
e: Vitamin D deficiency (limited sunlight) causes rickets, with bow legs.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) works mainly by promoting absorption of water along with:
e: Sodium-glucose co-transport drives water absorption, the basis of ORS.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: In a community living mostly on polished rice, some adults develop numbness and leg weakness (dry beriberi). The deficient nutrient is:
e: Polished rice lacks thiamine, whose deficiency causes beriberi.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: Body Mass Index (BMI) is calculated as:
e: BMI = weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) is used mainly to assess:
e: MUAC is a simple field measure of acute malnutrition (wasting) in children.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: On a growth chart, a child's weight line stays flat over three months. This indicates:
e: A flat or falling growth curve signals growth faltering and needs attention.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: The National Nutrition Mission of India is popularly known as:
e: POSHAN Abhiyaan is the National Nutrition Mission targeting malnutrition.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: Double-fortified salt is fortified with iodine and:
e: Double-fortified salt adds iron along with iodine to combat anaemia and goitre.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: A mother asks how much extra energy she needs while exclusively breastfeeding (first 6 months). Per ICMR it is about an additional:
e: ICMR recommends about +600 kcal/day during the first six months of lactation.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: The protein of the highest biological value (the reference protein) is found in:
e: Egg protein has the highest biological value and is used as the reference protein.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: Severe untreated Vitamin A deficiency can damage the cornea, a condition called:
e: Severe Vitamin A deficiency can progress to keratomalacia, leading to blindness.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: Iodine deficiency in the foetus or newborn can cause impaired growth and mental development known as:
e: Iodine deficiency in early life causes cretinism, with stunted growth and intellectual disability.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: An Anganwadi worker wants a cheap, locally available protein to enrich a weaning food. The best choice is:
e: Pulses and legumes are an inexpensive, widely available source of protein for weaning foods.
s: Section O - Nutrition & Community Health: Applied & Extended

q: A teacher gives a child a star each time he finishes his homework, and homework completion increases. This is:
e: Adding a pleasant consequence (a star) to increase behaviour is positive reinforcement.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: A toddler avoids touching the stove after being burned once. This illustrates learning through:
e: An unpleasant consequence (the burn) reduces the behaviour, an example of punishment.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: Parents take away a child's video-game time to stop her tantrums, and tantrums decrease. This is:
e: Removing a pleasant stimulus to reduce behaviour is negative punishment (response cost).
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: A student studies hard, which stops her parents' constant nagging; her studying then increases. This is:
e: Removing an unpleasant stimulus (nagging) to increase behaviour is negative reinforcement.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: A man angry at his boss comes home and shouts at his wife instead. This defence mechanism is:
e: Redirecting feelings from the real target to a safer one is displacement.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: A student who fails an exam insists the teacher was unfair, rather than admit he did not study. This defence mechanism is:
e: Offering plausible but false excuses to justify failure is rationalisation.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: Under stress, an adult begins biting his nails and sucking his thumb like a child. This defence mechanism is:
e: Reverting to an earlier, childish behaviour under stress is regression.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: A person channels aggressive urges into competitive sport. This mature defence mechanism is:
e: Redirecting unacceptable impulses into socially valued activity is sublimation.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: The part of Freud's personality that works on the 'pleasure principle' is the:
e: The id seeks immediate gratification on the pleasure principle.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: The part of Freud's personality that works on the 'reality principle' is the:
e: The ego mediates between the id and reality on the reality principle.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: The moral conscience component of Freud's personality is the:
e: The superego represents internalised morality and conscience.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: A child behaves well only to avoid being punished by the teacher. In Kohlberg's theory this is the:
e: Obeying to avoid punishment is pre-conventional moral reasoning.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: In Pavlov's experiment, after conditioning, the bell becomes the:
e: Through pairing, the bell becomes a conditioned stimulus that triggers salivation.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: In Pavlov's experiment, the food that naturally makes the dog salivate is the:
e: Food is the unconditioned stimulus because it triggers salivation without learning.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: Salivation produced by the bell alone (after conditioning) is the:
e: Salivation to the bell alone is the learned, conditioned response.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: A child bitten by one dog becomes frightened of all dogs. This spread of the response to similar stimuli is:
e: Responding similarly to stimuli resembling the original is stimulus generalisation.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: Thorndike's principle that responses followed by satisfaction are strengthened is the:
e: The Law of Effect states that rewarding consequences strengthen a response.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: Spearman's theory of intelligence proposed a single general factor called:
e: Spearman proposed a general intelligence factor, 'g'.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: The theory of 'multiple intelligences' was proposed by:
e: Howard Gardner proposed that there are several relatively independent intelligences.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: If a person's IQ is exactly 100, it means the person's mental age:
e: An IQ of 100 means mental age equals chronological age.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: According to the Cannon-Bard theory of emotion, physiological arousal and the felt emotion occur:
e: Cannon-Bard holds that arousal and emotion occur at the same time.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: The Schachter-Singer (two-factor) theory says emotion arises from physiological arousal plus:
e: In the two-factor theory, we interpret (label) our arousal to experience a specific emotion.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: Organising what we see into a main 'figure' against a 'background' is a principle of:
e: Figure-ground organisation is a key Gestalt principle of perception.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: Still images shown in rapid succession are perceived as smooth motion (as in films). This illusion is the:
e: The phi phenomenon is the perception of apparent motion from rapidly presented still images.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: The memory process of bringing stored information back into awareness is called:
e: Retrieval is recovering stored information when needed.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: The tendency to recall the first items in a list better than the middle ones is the:
e: Better recall of the earliest items is the primacy effect.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: During revision, a student best remembers the first and last topics she studied. This is the:
e: Superior recall of items at both ends of a list is the serial position effect.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: When newly learned information makes it harder to recall older information, it is called:
e: Retroactive interference is when new learning disrupts memory of older material.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: The personality types 'introvert' and 'extravert' were introduced by:
e: Carl Jung introduced the introvert-extravert distinction.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: Which of the following is one of the 'Big Five' personality traits?
e: The Big Five are openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: The Rorschach test assesses personality using:
e: The Rorschach is a projective test based on responses to inkblots.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: A psychologist shows a client ambiguous pictures and asks her to make up a story about each. This projective test is the:
e: The TAT uses ambiguous pictures to reveal personality through the stories told.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: Excessive, uncontrollable worry about many everyday matters for at least six months suggests:
e: Persistent, free-floating worry for six months or more characterises Generalised Anxiety Disorder.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: A boy repeatedly washes his hands and re-checks his bag, feeling intense distress if he tries to stop. This suggests:
e: Recurrent intrusive thoughts and repetitive rituals point to obsessive-compulsive disorder.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: A specific learning disability that mainly affects reading is:
e: Dyslexia is a specific learning disability affecting reading.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: An intelligent 8-year-old reads far below grade level despite normal teaching and effort. This most likely indicates:
e: A marked gap between ability and reading achievement points to a specific learning disability.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: A childhood disorder marked by persistent aggression, lying, stealing and serious rule-violation is:
e: Conduct disorder involves a repetitive pattern of violating others' rights and major rules.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: A researcher studies the same group of children at ages 3, 6 and 9. This research design is:
e: Following the same individuals over time is a longitudinal design.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: Comparing different age groups, all studied at one point in time, is a:
e: Studying several age groups at one time is a cross-sectional design.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: The debate over the relative roles of heredity and environment in development is called the:
e: The nature-nurture debate concerns the contributions of heredity versus environment.
s: Section P - Psychology: Learning, Motivation & Cognition (Applied)

q: A social worker helps a grieving widow one-to-one to cope with her loss. The method used is:
e: Helping an individual through a one-to-one professional relationship is social casework.
s: Section R - Social Work & Child Welfare: Applied & Extended

q: A worker forms a group of adolescents to build confidence and life skills through shared activities. The method is:
e: Using a group as the medium for members' growth is social group work.
s: Section R - Social Work & Child Welfare: Applied & Extended

q: A worker mobilises the residents of a slum to jointly demand a clean water supply. The method is:
e: Helping a community organise to meet a common need is community organisation.
s: Section R - Social Work & Child Welfare: Applied & Extended

q: A worker leads a public campaign and petition to change a discriminatory rule. The method is:
e: Organised collective effort to bring social change is social action.
s: Section R - Social Work & Child Welfare: Applied & Extended

q: A caseworker listens to a distressed client with warmth but keeps professional objectivity. This reflects the principle of:
